_readme: Copy library for the seven lifecycle emails. PostHog holds only whichever variant is currently live on each step - this file is the source of truth and its git history is the record of every decision the weekly loop has made. build_email.py turns an entry here into the exact payload workflows-patch-action-email expects; decide.py chooses which entry that should be; optimise.md is the runbook the scheduled job follows. Exactly one variant per step is 'champion' and at most one is 'testing'; two can never be live at once because PostHog has no split node, which is why the test is sequential - see the top of decide.py for what that costs.

_angles.utility: No persuasion. Tells them the one thing to do and gets out of the way.
_angles.question: Subject is a real question. Questions are the highest-opening subject format measured (~46%), and a reply is the cleanest engagement signal there is.
_angles.specific: Concrete number or outcome in the subject. Specific curiosity beats vague teasing by ~26%; vague teasing also wins opens and loses clicks.
_angles.empathy: Names the awkwardness out loud. Beats urgency on win-back - 'did we lose you' outperforms 'final notice'.
_angles.confession: Leads with something that went wrong on our side. The register that earned 29% replies on the old campaign.
_angles.peer: Speaks in another user's voice rather than the company's. Unlocks accounts that company-voice email cannot.
_angles.permission: Offers to stop emailing. Counter-intuitively strong on dormant lists and cleans the list either way.
_angles.research: Ask to buy their time, not their money. The offer is credits for an interview; the conversion that matters is a booked call, so the click is the result.

The people who get the most out of LinkFinder mostly stop using the web app. They take the API key from their account page and call it from wherever their list already lives, or they paste the MCP URL into Claude and ask for contacts in the chat.
The web app is the demo. The API and the MCP server are the product, and you already have both.

Contact data decays about 2% a month - people change jobs, emails bounce, numbers get reassigned. The half-finished list sitting in your account is worth slightly less today than it was on Tuesday, and it will keep going that way.
The smallest top-up is $25 and never expires. That is usually enough to finish what you started.

So here is a straight trade: give me fifteen minutes to hear what you were trying to build, and I will put 1,000 credits on your account. That is the $25 pack, free, whether or not you ever buy anything.

A verified email is 10 credits. On the $25 pack that is 2.5 cents. On Starter it is under a tenth of a cent. A researcher doing it by hand costs you somewhere north of a dollar a contact and gets it wrong more often.

People who hit the export gate paid at 9.5%, uploaders who did not at 4.2%, one-at-a-time users at 0.35%. This email exists to move people into that 241.

body: Hi — Eliasse again.
Most people find LinkFinder, run a couple of lookups, and then quietly go back to doing the rest by hand. That is the part I would like to save you.

You can drop in a CSV — names and companies, or a column of LinkedIn URLs — and get the whole list back enriched. A hundred rows takes about as long as the two you did by hand. There is a sample list in the app if you do not have one ready: one click and you can watch it run.
It is included in what you already have. Nothing to buy to try it.

body: I looked at what separates the people who get real value out of LinkFinder from the ones who drift off after a few lookups.

It is not the plan they are on or how long they have had an account. It is whether they ever uploaded a list. Almost everyone who sticks around found the bulk upload early; almost everyone who left never did.
